senses: A gold coin used in the Ottoman Empire.
examples: His ready cash consisted of eight hundred thousand mahbub and funduclys; the rest of his treasure was in jewels, to the amount of about six million of ducats.
The only coins allowed by the Turkish government to be struck at Cairo are the Mahbub (or Zermahbub) Sequins, and Medini.
At Grand Cairo in Egypt, contracts are made in funducli and mahbub sequins; the former are reckoned at 146 medini, and 3 mahbubs are equal to 4 pataccas, so that the mahbub is worth 120 medini.

senses: One who, or that which, reclines.
A chair hinged so that the back can be reclined for comfort.
Thin, translucent, gelatinous traditional Japanese noodles made from the Asian plant konjac.
Hanging from, or as if from, a support.
Indecisive or hesitant
ety: Borrowed from Latin pendulus (“pendant”), from pendeō (“to hang”).

senses: A quick and sketchy drawing, often of a live model. Croquis drawings are usually made in a few minutes, after which the model changes pose and another croquis is drawn.
The epitome of physical and intellectual achievement to which an Ancient Greek citizen could aspire; societal and cultural perfection.
An early model of Christian higher learning having theology as its chief subject.
A pedagogical system focusing on providing children with a broad and balanced education.
ety: From Ancient Greek παιδείᾱ (paideíā, “rearing of a child, education”), from παιδεύω (paideúō, “rear a child”) + -ίᾱ (-íā), from παῖς (paîs, “child”).

senses: A sheep of a Central Asian breed.
A type of hat made from the wool of these sheep.
ety: Named after the town Qorakoʻl, from Uzbek, meaning black lake.

senses: Of a sound, quality, or characteristic, that a person cannot listen to for an extended time.
examples: Many older adults find rap music unlistenable.

senses: A small, often seasoned, piece of dry or fried bread.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from French croûton. Compare croute.

senses: The art and science of gems.
A person who has had one or more limbs removed.
ety: From French amputée, (past participle of amputer (“to amputate”)), from Latin amputatus, perfect passive participle of amputare (“to amputate”).

senses: A monastic or similar religious establishment in Hinduism and Jainism, usually more formal and hierarchical than an ashram.
A plasterer.
examples: Can not a Pargeter make a browne wal white?

senses: A type of terracotta given a red colour by its concentration of ferrous oxide.
The act of making, or treating as, financial; bringing something into the sphere of finance.
A doctor specializing in the treatment of arthritis and other ailments of the joints.
Resembling or characteristic of a python (snake).
examples: The Indians of the Amazon consider the Mai d’agoa, a pythonesque snake, to be the guardian of the Wild Lake of the Amazon.
Two fire signs, talented Aries and intelligent snake, combine to make a more powerful, pythonesque snake.
I saw my middle-aged brother stuffing a garter snake through a tiny hole in the screen, the snake inflating, pythonesque.

senses: Able or needing to be registered.
examples: Every mortgage of land evidenced in writing is registrable with the Land Office.

senses: That occurs around the time of labor and childbirth (parturition) (typically, within a few weeks before, intrapartum, or within a few weeks after).
ety: From peri- + Latin partum (“giving birth”), thus "around [the time of] birth".

senses: The state of being special, exceptional or unique.
A philosophy of prevention or of intervention.
Dated spelling of lagoon.
ety: Borrowed from French lagune, from Venetan laguna, from Latin lacūna.

senses: One who brews his or her own beer or other alcoholic beverage; one who homebrews.
An amateur who builds radio equipment or develops video games, etc.
Somewhat warm.
Scientific; of or pertaining to science.
Apparently, but not necessarily, scientific; having the trappings of science.
ety: From science + -y (“characterized by; like”, suffix forming an adjective).
examples: True, most of us concede that quasi-experimental empirical research, today symbolized by multiple-regression equations, is in some sense the most "sciencey" part of political science.
AIDS was too sciencey for me. My eighth-grade term paper was on censorship, Tipper Gore's assault on free speech in the music industry, and the Dead Kennedys.
But with the statement above, I honestly can't recall a situation where it wasn't true although I have no sciencey data to back this up.

senses: A Venezuelan genre of music with African influences and drumming.
examples: The nonpurist result is world-music fusion, linking the Central American parranda and punta to African and Latin pop, flamenco, even electric blues.

senses: A liquid crystal having the molecules aligned in this way; a phase of a liquid crystal in which the molecules are so aligned.
ety: From Latin smecticus, from Ancient Greek σμηκτικός (smēktikós), from σμήχειν (smḗkhein, “to wipe, to cleanse”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”).

senses: prone to cheating.
Involving cheating; fraudulent.

senses: Pompous, officious talk.

ety: From Middle English blusteren (“to wander about aimlessly”); however, apparently picking up the modern sense from Middle Low German blüstren (“to blow violently”; compare later Low German blustern, blistern). Related to blow, blast. Compare also Saterland Frisian bloasje (“to blow”), bruusje (“to bluster”).

senses: Having or indicating wish or desire.

A space on a paper form that can be optionally filled with a check mark.
